t: Minimize Maximum of Array — Greedy Prefix Average
o: Operations move one unit from index i to i-1 — mass only flows leftward. Therefore for any prefix [0..i], the total sum is invariant under operations internal to the prefix, and the minimum achievable maximum on that prefix is ceil(sum/(i+1)). The final answer is the max over all prefixes of ceil(prefix_i/(i+1)), because a large early prefix can never be relieved by later elements. Example 1: prefixes give ceil(3/1)=3, ceil(10/2)=5, ceil(11/3)=4, ceil(17/4)=5 → answer 5. Example 2: ceil(10/1)=10 dominates.
k: Units move only toward smaller indices, so each prefix's sum is a lower bound on its max: max >= ceil(prefixSum/(len)).
That bound is achievable simultaneously for all prefixes by greedily leveling left-to-right.
Answer = max over i of ceil(sum(nums[0..i]) / (i+1)); no binary search needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Running Sum
a.i: Scan left to right accumulating the prefix sum; at each index the best possible cap for the prefix is ceil(s/(i+1)). Taking the maximum of these caps gives the answer: it is a valid lower bound (prefix argument), and a constructive leveling argument shows it is attainable — process i from 1 upward, moving excess of nums[i] over the current cap into nums[i-1].
s: For each i: s += nums[i]; candidate = ceil(s/(i+1)).
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) work per element.

w: Use 64-bit accumulation: sums reach 1e14. The ceiling trick (s+i)/(i+1) avoids floating point. Common mistake: answering max prefix average only over the full array, or trying a local-swap simulation that misses the prefix lower bound. Follow-up: prove achievability formally by induction on the greedy leveling, or handle the variant where moves cost something.
